analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for coal miners with black lung disease to win and keep federal benefits, and makes coal companies pay more of the cost.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 16, 2025 with 5 Democratic cosponsors and referred to two House committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul the federal program that pays disability benefits to coal miners disabled by black lung disease and to their families. It would give miners free government-funded medical evaluations (including CT scans), create an automatic approval for miners with advanced disease on their scans, pay lawyers' fees for claims that drag past two years, restore annual inflation increases that were frozen out of benefit checks, let miners reopen claims that were denied using medical opinions later discredited, and require coal companies that self-insure to prove they are financially able to pay, with much larger penalties when they don't.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners and surviving spouses with black lung disease, a group whose disease rates are rising again after decades of decline. Miners with complicated pneumoconiosis would get benefits almost automatically when a qualifying CT scan, X-ray, biopsy, or autopsy shows it, and government-paid evaluations would remove the cost of proving a claim. Families would see benefit checks rise with inflation starting in 2026, instead of staying flat when federal pay is frozen. Miners whose earlier claims were denied based on readings from doctors later discredited by the Labor Department could reopen their cases and collect back pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners and their surviving spouses

how_it_helps.text: Miners with an X-ray, CT scan, biopsy, or autopsy showing complicated pneumoconiosis (progressive massive fibrosis) would be presumed totally disabled due to black lung, a presumption coal companies could not rebut except by proving the lesion has a different cause [S2].

The Labor Department would provide a free 'complete pulmonary evaluation' at claimant request, including CT scans in defined circumstances, paid from the trust fund and reimbursed by the liable coal operator if benefits are awarded [S2].

The Department would maintain a public list of qualified physicians, screening out doctors with disciplinary records and barring, for 24 months, doctors retained by coal companies or their lawyers from doing claimant evaluations [S2].

Benefit rates would reset to $10,769 per year starting in 2026 and rise each year with the Consumer Price Index; under current law benefits are tied to a federal pay grade and were frozen in multiple years [S2].

Miners and survivors whose claims were denied based on a chest X-ray read by a physician the Secretary has discredited could file a new claim, have it decided without that reading, and collect benefits back to the original denial or the miner's death [S2].

A new program would pay approved attorneys' fees (up to $4,500) and unreimbursed medical expenses (up to $3,000) from the trust fund for contested claims not resolved within two years, addressing a process where, per GAO findings cited in the bill, only 42% of claimants have a lawyer at the initial stage [S2].

Coal operators would have to meet financial-health criteria to self-insure their black lung liabilities, penalties for failing to secure payment would rise from $1,000 to $25,000, and executives and commonly controlled businesses would be liable for the full actuarial value of defaulted benefits [S2].
The Labor Secretary would have to submit a strategy to reduce the backlog of pending cases, targeting average case resolution in under 12 months [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face a higher bar to self-insure, larger penalties for failing to secure their obligations, personal and affiliate liability when a company defaults, and reimbursement of the trust fund for claimants' medical evaluation costs and program-paid legal fees when benefits are awarded. The Black Lung Disability Trust Fund fronts the new costs in the meantime; it is financed by a tax on coal, so costs can flow back to the industry, and any shortfall ultimately draws on taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill increases federal outlays: the benefit reset to $10,769 per year, CPI indexing, free medical evaluations, and the legal-fee program are all charged to the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund first, and the bill includes no new revenue to cover them [S2].

The irrebuttable presumption of total disability for miners with lesions over 1 centimeter is a strong expansion of eligibility; while the bill allows a showing that the lesion has a non-pneumoconiosis cause, an honest supporter would acknowledge this shifts many close cases toward automatic award [S2].

Stricter self-insurance criteria, a 25-fold penalty increase, and 'other responsible party' liability reaching affiliates and executives raise compliance costs for coal operators, and those costs can be passed into coal prices and electricity rates [S2].

Claimant-side provisions apply only one way in practice: the new criminal and attorney-disqualification penalties for false statements cover everyone, but the burden of the expanded adjudication process falls on the operators and the fund [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is aimed at a documented problem: a complex, adversarial claims process that claimants often cannot navigate, benefits that lost ground to inflation, and self-insured companies that defaulted and shifted costs to the public trust fund. The design leans strongly toward claimants, and the added costs are real but mostly redirected onto the industry Congress intended to bear them; the main fiscal risk is the un-funded gap between the new trust-fund obligations and the coal tax that pays for them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, and so far neither has taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan McGarvey introduced the Black Lung Benefits Improvement Act of 2025 in the House on December 16, 2025 [S1].
The Speaker referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over its provisions [S4].
Five House Democrats have cosponsored it; no Republican has [S3].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; the bill sits in committee awaiting action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill awaits committee action

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters in the record, including the sponsor, are House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; the committees that would act on it are controlled by Republicans who have not scheduled it.

industries.note: Operators would face stricter self-insurance requirements, penalties raised from $1,000 to $25,000 for failing to secure benefits, liability reaching executives and commonly controlled businesses when a company defaults, and reimbursement of the trust fund for claimants' evaluation and legal costs. These costs exist because operators' obligations to sick miners have frequently gone unpaid or shifted to the public fund [S2].

industries.industry: Company-retained medical experts and physicians (chest X-ray 'B readers')
industries.note: The bill lets the Labor Secretary disregard X-ray interpretations by physicians it has discredited, reopen those claims, and bar physicians retained by coal companies or their lawyers within the prior 24 months from performing claimant evaluations. This targets doctors whose company-paid readings have historically helped deny claims [S2].
A new fund-paid program would cover attorneys' fees and medical-expense costs in contested claims unresolved after two years, addressing the fact that most claimants go unrepresented [S2].

The fund pays for the new benefits, evaluations, and fees up front, but the self-insurance and penalty provisions are designed to push liabilities back onto operators, improving the fund's long-term finances [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill is at the earliest stage: referred to two committees with only Democratic support so far. Most bills never get a committee markup, and the majority has not signaled interest, so the likely path is that it sits unless a committee schedules a hearing or elements are folded into broader legislation. Black lung issues have drawn bipartisan concern in past Congresses because the affected miners are concentrated in coal states represented by both parties, which gives it a narrow path beyond pure party-line odds.
